item.title: Eastern North Pacific Tropical Weather Outlook
item.description:
883
ABPZ20 KNHC 252309
TWOEP

Tropical Weather Outlook
NWS National Hurricane Center Miami FL
500 PM PDT Sun Oct 25 2026

For the eastern and central North Pacific east of 180 longitude:

Active Systems:
The National Hurricane Center is issuing advisories on recently
downgraded Tropical Storm Vance, located a few hundred miles
west-southwest of Acapulco, Mexico, and on recently upgraded
Tropical Storm Olana, located several hundred miles west-southwest
of Johnston Atoll.

Tropical cyclone formation is not expected over the next 7 days.

&&
Public Advisories on Tropical Storm Olana are issued under
WMO header WTPA33 KNHC and under AWIPS header HFOTCPCP3.
Forecast/Advisories on Tropical Storm Olana are issued under
WMO header WTPA23 KNHC and under AWIPS header HFOTCMCP3.

$$
Forecaster Katz/Cangialosi

item.title: Tropical Storm Vance Public Advisory Number 19
item.description:
Issued at 900 PM CST Sun Oct 25 2026 
000
WTPZ32 KNHC 260236
TCPEP2
 
BULLETIN
Tropical Storm Vance Advisory Number  19
NWS National Hurricane Center Miami FL       EP222026
900 PM CST Sun Oct 25 2026
 
...VANCE CONTINUES TO WEAKEN AS THE STORM MOVES TO THE
NORTHWEST...
 
 
SUMMARY OF 900 PM CST...0300 UTC...INFORMATION
----------------------------------------------
LOCATION...15.0N 104.7W
ABOUT 345 MI...555 KM WSW OF ACAPULCO MEXICO
ABOUT 275 MI...445 KM S OF MANZANILLO MEXICO
MAXIMUM SUSTAINED WINDS...65 MPH...100 KM/H
PRESENT MOVEMENT...NW OR 305 DEGREES AT 7 MPH...11 KM/H
MINIMUM CENTRAL PRESSURE...995 MB...29.39 INCHES
 
 
WATCHES AND WARNINGS
--------------------
There are no coastal watches or warnings in effect.
 
Interests along the southwestern coast of Mexico should monitor the
progress of Vance.
 
 
DISCUSSION AND OUTLOOK
----------------------
At 900 PM CST (0300 UTC), the center of Tropical Storm Vance was 
located near latitude 15.0 North, longitude 104.7 West. Vance is 
moving toward the northwest near 7 mph (11 km/h). A 
west-northwestward motion at a slower forward speed is expected over 
the next couple of days, followed by a turn toward the north around 
midweek.
 
Maximum sustained winds have decreased to near 65 mph (100 km/h) 
with higher gusts. Gradual weakening is forecast for the next 
several days. 

Tropical-storm-force winds extend outward up to 150 miles (240 km)
from the center.
 
The estimated minimum central pressure is 995 mb (29.39 inches).
 
 
HAZARDS AFFECTING LAND
----------------------
RAINFALL: Through Thursday, Vance is expected to produce 2 to 4
inches of rain, with isolated higher totals of 7 inches possible,
across Colima, Nayarit, and Sinaloa, along with western portions of
Michoacán, Jalisco, and Durango. This rainfall may produce flooding
and mudslides, especially in areas along steep terrain.
 
For a complete depiction of forecast rainfall associated with Vance,
please see the National Weather Service Storm Total Rainfall Graphic
available at hurricanes.gov/graphics_ep2.shtml?rainqpf.
 
SURF: Swells generated by Vance will affect portions of the coast of
southern and southwestern Mexico during the next several days. These
swells are likely to cause life-threatening surf and rip current
conditions. Please consult products from your local weather office.
 
 
NEXT ADVISORY
-------------
Next complete advisory at 300 AM CST.
 
$$
Forecaster Katz/Cangialosi

item.title: Tropical Storm Vance Forecast Discussion Number 19
item.description:
Issued at 900 PM CST Sun Oct 25 2026 
000
WTPZ42 KNHC 260237
TCDEP2
 
Tropical Storm Vance Discussion Number  19
NWS National Hurricane Center Miami FL       EP222026
900 PM CST Sun Oct 25 2026
 
Vance's structure continues to degrade as seen in visible satellite
imagery and the GPM and AMSR3 microwave passes, due to strong
vertical wind shear and relatively dry mid-level air. Convection
continues to develop to the northeast of the center, but it is
mostly limited to that quadrant. The TAFB Dvorak fix was T3.5/55 kt
and the objective intensity estimates from UW-CIMSS are in 37-52 kt
range.  Based on that data, the initial intensity has been lowered
to 55 kt.
 
Vance is currently moving toward the northwest, 305/6 kt. The
tropical storm is being steered by a mid-level ridge centered over
the south-central United States, along with a closed upper-level low
moving across the southwestern United States. The cyclone is
expected to continue to move toward the northwest to west-northwest
with a decrease in forward speed as the steering currents weaken. A
turn back to the north is expected by the middle of the week as an
amplified mid to upper-level trough moves over the eastern Pacific.
The current NHC track forecast has been adjusted a little to the
west of the previous one. Future adjustments to the west are likely
if the guidance trends continue.
 
The combination of southwesterly wind shear and relatively dry
mid-level air are expected to continue to gradually weaken the
storm. By the middle of this week, an upper-level trough will
further enhance the wind shear, resulting in additional weakening.
Both the GFS and ECMWF simulated satellite imagery suggest that
Vance will struggle to hold on to organized deep convection by late
this week. The current intensity forecast still calls for Vance
to become post-tropical at 96 h and degenerate into a remnant low by
120 h. However, the current intensity forecast is on the upper end
of the guidance envelope, as most of the guidance shows the rate of
weakening much faster than what is currently forecast. It is
certainly possible that the cyclone could weaken faster, which will
mean that it could become a remnant low sooner than what is
forecasted.
 
Key Messages:
 
1. Although the threat to southwest Mexico is decreasing
as the forecast track shifts westward away from the coast,
interests there should continue to monitor Vance's progress.
 
2. Periods of heavy rainfall associated with Vance will impact
portions of western Mexico during much of this week. This rainfall
may produce flooding and mudslides across Colima, Nayarit, and
Sinaloa, along with western portions of Michoacán, Jalisco, and
Durango, especially in areas along steep terrain.
